description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing gaps in the network guard's coverage — missing benchmarking and test-net ranges in IPv4, plus unchecked NAT64-embedded IPv4 addresses in IPv6, though these are relatively low-risk cases.

A more concerning bypass emerges with the mapped hex form "::ffff:7f00:1": since the mapped regex only matches dotted notation, this literal address slips past isBlockedIpv6 entirely, and net.isIP confirms it's a valid address. On dual-stack Linux sockets, connecting to this address actually routes to 127.0.0.1, meaning Node would create an AF_INET6 socket that the kernel silently maps to IPv4 loopback — a genuine SSRF bypass since extractHost keeps this host string and resolvePublicHost never flags it as blocked.

But I need to check how the WHATWG URL parser handles this: when parsing "http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/", the hostname gets normalized to "[::ffff:7f00:1]" with brackets included, which would fail isPlausibleHost's checks since bracketed forms don't match net.isIP or the regex. So the actual exploitability depends heavily on which code path (raw host string vs URL parsing) processes the input — I should trace through each route carefully to confirm where the gap actually exists.

I also need to check whether resolvePublicHost's vetted IP is actually what gets connected to, or if fetch() re-resolves DNS afterward, which would enable rebinding, and whether redirect-following in fetch bypasses the SSRF guard entirely. Time to read through the route handlers directly.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that most routes are POST-only, so testing might require one careful read-only-style call if it doesn't write to the database — I should check whether rate limiting is in-memory or persisted, and confirm the WHOIS lookup only follows a single referral from IANA to the registrar.

I'm also thinking through edge cases in the WHOIS flow: the IANA fallback could misleadingly report TLD-level dates as if they belonged to the domain, and some newer gTLDs no longer support WHOIS at all after ICANN's 2025 sunset in favor of RDAP, which could break lookups for those domains.

I'm realizing the naive prefix match on "registrar" is order-dependent and fragile — for example.com's Verisign record, the first "registrar"-prefixed field encountered is "Registrar WHOIS Server: whois.iana.org", which would get grabbed instead of the actual registrar name field.

content.content:
import type { NodeProvider } from "@prisma/client";

/**
 * Valid datacenter-code per provider, plus a human-readable label for each.
 * `Node.region` is a plain string (not an enum) because datacenter codes
 * grow far more often than providers do — same "fast-changing categorical
 * value, validated in code not the DB" convention this schema already uses
 * for StaffGrant.area (see lib/staff-grants.ts). Validate any new/edited
 * Node's region against `NODE_REGIONS[provider]` rather than trusting a
 * free-typed string from the admin form.
 *
 * Codes are each provider's OWN real datacenter code (OVH's/Hetzner's own
 * naming), not a platform-invented scheme — "sgp1" (OVH Singapore, where the
 * primary node actually is — confirmed via geoip-lite against its live
 * public IP, not guessed) and "fsn1" (Hetzner Falkenstein, Germany, the new
 * node) are both real. The other codes below are real provider datacenter
 * codes too, listed so the region field has somewhere to grow without a
 * schema change — add more here as real nodes are added, not speculatively.
 */
export const NODE_REGIONS: Record<NodeProvider, string[]> = {
  OVH: ["sgp1", "bhs1", "gra1", "rbx1", "waw1"],
  HETZNER: ["fsn1", "nbg1", "hel1", "ash1", "hil1"],
};

export const REGION_LABELS: Record<string, string> = {
  sgp1: "Singapore",
  bhs1: "Beauharnois, CA",
  gra1: "Gravelines, FR",
  rbx1: "Roubaix, FR",
  waw1: "Warsaw, PL",
  fsn1: "Falkenstein, DE",
  nbg1: "Nuremberg, DE",
  hel1: "Helsinki, FI",
  ash1: "Ashburn, US",
  hil1: "Hillsboro, US",
};

/**
 * Customer-facing location labels — deliberately simpler than REGION_LABELS
 * above. A customer picking where their server lives doesn't need (and often
 * won't recognize) the exact datacenter city — "Falkenstein, DE" confused
 * customers who don't know it's the small German town OVH/Hetzner's
 * Falkenstein facility sits in. REGION_LABELS stays as-is for admin/ops
 * screens, where the precise city genuinely matters (e.g. telling apart two
 * German facilities, fsn1 vs nbg1, if both are ever in use at once).
 */
export const CUSTOMER_REGION_LABELS: Record<string, string> = {
  sgp1: "Singapore",
  bhs1: "Canada",
  gra1: "France",
  rbx1: "France",
  waw1: "Poland",
  fsn1: "Germany",
  nbg1: "Germany",
  hel1: "Finland",
  ash1: "United States",
  hil1: "United States",
};

export function customerRegionLabel(region: string): string {
  return CUSTOMER_REGION_LABELS[region] ?? REGION_LABELS[region] ?? region;
}

/** ISO2 country code per region, for a flag icon next to a location card (optional UI nicety). */
export const REGION_COUNTRY: Record<string, string> = {
  sgp1: "sg",
  bhs1: "ca",
  gra1: "fr",
  rbx1: "fr",
  waw1: "pl",
  fsn1: "de",
  nbg1: "de",
  hel1: "fi",
  ash1: "us",
  hil1: "us",
};

export function isValidRegion(provider: NodeProvider, region: string): boolean {
  return NODE_REGIONS[provider]?.includes(region) ?? false;
}

---
name: nxeon-brand-voice-no-provider
description: "Never say \"our provider\"/\"our infrastructure partner\" etc. to Nxeon customers — Nxeon presents itself as the infrastructure owner, not a reseller"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc
  modified: 2026-08-29T15:18:19.380Z
---

Never use phrasing like "our provider," "our infrastructure partner," "our network provider," or any language that implies Nxeon depends on a third party for its core infrastructure, in any customer-facing communication (support tickets, emails, UI copy, chat responses). Nxeon must always speak in its own voice as if it fully owns and operates its infrastructure — "our network," "our systems," "our DDoS protection," never "our provider's X."

**Why:** On 2026-08-29, in a support-ticket reply about DDoS protection capacity, I wrote "Our provider's stated policy is explicit on this..." — the user corrected this immediately: "you should never mention to customer 'our Provider' or 'OVH' in their eyes, we don't have a provider, we are the provider. it devalues our company image." This is stricter than just "don't name the vendor" (already established in [[nxeon-multi-registrar-plan]]-adjacent work for hiding registrar identity) — even a generic, unnamed reference to "a provider" undermines the brand positioning that Nxeon owns its stack end-to-end. The correct phrasing was already used in the SAME thread's first reply ("Our network-level DDoS filtering operates...") — that's the model to follow.

**How to apply:** Before sending any customer-facing text that describes infrastructure, security, or capacity, scan for "provider," "partner," "vendor," "upstream," or similar reseller-revealing language and rewrite in first-person-owner voice. This applies even when the underlying technical fact is genuinely sourced from a real hosting/network partner (e.g. OVH) — the vendor's name must never appear (established separately), AND the fact that a vendor exists at all must not be implied either. Research/verify real technical facts from the actual vendor's documentation as needed (that's still correct and necessary for accuracy — see the DDoS-capacity ticket work), but always present the resulting capability as Nxeon's own when relaying it to a customer.

content.thinking:
I want to verify the SSRF hex-mapped IPv6 bypass idea offline by mimicking the isBlockedIpv6 logic in a scratch script rather than the real project code. Tracing extractHost with "::ffff:7f00:1" through the port-checker logic, it isn't URL-like, doesn't start with a bracket, and since it contains a colon and net.isIP reports it as version 6, the IPv4-mapped check gets skipped entirely.

Following through resolvePublicHost, the address isn't in BLOCKED_NAMES, passes isPlausibleHost since net.isIP recognizes it, and then hits isBlockedIpv6 — but the mapped-IPv4 regex doesn't match this form, it's not "::1", and parsing the head segment yields 0 rather than an fc/fe prefix, so the check returns false and the address is allowed through unblocked. That means tryConnect can actually reach it: on Linux, connecting to "::ffff:7f00:1" over IPv6 dual-stack resolves to 127.0.0.1, letting port-checker probe local services like Proxmox, the app, Postgres, and Redis, plus reach internal 10.20.0.x hosts via their mapped equivalents. The mc-status tool has the same exposure, and ssl-checker would leak local TLS certs the same way — though http-headers happens to be safe here since the bracketed IPv6 hostname form fails the isPlausibleHost check and gets rejected outright.

I'm also checking other IPv6 forms — "::ffff:0:7f00:1" isn't routed since it's IPv4-translated, NAT64 addresses require a gateway that's unlikely to exist, and IPv4-compatible addresses aren't routed to v4 on Linux, so the "::ffff:hex" form remains the main vector; uppercase variants get lowercased and still match the blocklist regex correctly. Then I look at IPv4 edge cases: hex-octet and decimal-integer forms like "0x7f.0.0.1" or "2130706433" aren't recognized by net.isIP but do pass the hostname regex, triggering a DNS lookup that glibc resolves to 127.0.0.1 — and since the code checks resolved addresses afterward, these get blocked correctly. Now I'm wondering about the case where a hostname's AAAA record itself resolves to "::ffff:127.0.0.1" through DNS rather than a literal.

I confirm that inet_ntop formats v4-mapped addresses in dotted form, so DNS-resolved cases get caught by the regex, meaning only the literal hardcoded hex form actually bypasses detection since extractHost leaves it untouched. Then I consider whether Node's networking layer would actually let a connection to "::ffff:7f00:1" succeed — since Linux permits v4-mapped connects on AF_INET6 sockets unless IPV6_V6ONLY is set, this should work by default, and I don't think disabling IPv6 system-wide would block it either since v4-mapped connections route through the IPv4 stack regardless. To be sure, I want to write a standalone script that mirrors the isBlockedIpv6 logic and actually attempts the connection to confirm this behavior without touching anything in production.

I decide to keep this test purely local — connecting to my own machine's SSH port using the mapped address is harmless and doesn't require exploiting the live API's SSRF vulnerability, since the rules only permit one benign POST request with something like example.com. I'll verify the bypass logic locally instead. I also note that for multi-address DNS resolution the code just uses the first address, which seems fine, and that the DNS tool's plausibility check relies on the system resolver rather than resolvePublicHost — it filters private A/AAAA records but doesn't filter CNAME, MX, NS, or TXT records, which could leak internal information.

I check the WHOIS tool: it opens a connection to the referral server using a hostname from the IANA response, which isn't SSRF-guarded but comes from a trusted source, and the user-controlled query is validated through extractHost and isPlausibleHost so CRLF injection isn't possible; sequential timeouts could add up to ten seconds total, which seems acceptable. For the Minecraft status tool, SRV lookups return attacker-controlled DNS targets, but those still pass through resolvePublicHost afterward, so I consider whether a malicious SRV target could smuggle something like an IPv4-mapped address through DNS label encoding — it's an edge case not worth pursuing further, so I note it as low risk. I also confirm that when a port is explicitly given, the SRV lookup step is skipped entirely.

I'm now more concerned about the latency figures being measured from the Singapore-based server without disclosing that origin, which could mislead a US player checking a US server into thinking their connection is laggy — a medium-low severity issue that also applies to the port-checker's latency readings. I verify the JSON response parsing and read timeout logic for server pings look fine, and that the sweep check correctly happens after resolvePublicHost, with blocked requests properly returning a 403 shown in the UI. I also flag the UDP and SRV record claims made in the data file, and start reviewing the call-to-action links across tool pages — most route to /vps via the shared ToolShell sidebar, while a few tools like latency, server-size, and the domain generator have their own inline CTAs pointing to pricing or domain registration flows.

content.text:
I audited all 16 tools and made 30 live requests, one at a time. Every tool page returns 200 and every API responds, but there is one Critical issue and four High ones. The Minecraft status page shows fake review ratings and made-up testimonials. The address filter that stops tool APIs reaching internal hosts can be bypassed. The latency test says Nxeon only has Singapore, but Germany is on sale. The size calculator contradicts Nxeon's own plans and prices. And an anonymous visitor who clicks "Register" in the domain generator loses the domain.

Nothing was changed on the server. The POST lookups only touch in-memory rate-limit counters and caches, and write no database rows. The single domain-generator call made one registrar availability check (name.com and Namecheap) and no Claude call. I did not fire the address-filter bypass at production; I proved it with a copy of the filter logic and a local connect.

## Findings, by priority

**1. Critical — fake review scores and invented testimonials on the live `/tools/minecraft-server-status`.**
- **Evidence:** the live HTML shows "4.9 out of 5 on Trustpilot — 312 reviews", "4.8 on HostAdvice — 148" and "4.9 on Google — 205", each twice. The badges link to `#`. The database has 0 rows in `Review` and no `review_url_*` settings, so `ReviewBadges.tsx:29-33` falls back to its demo figures. The demo badges carry no visible label, even though the code comment calls them "clearly-labelled". Testimonials from "mika.exe" and "Jordan P." (`tooltemplate/data.ts:41-44`, rendered at `ToolLanding.tsx:387`) are also live.
- **Why it matters:** this breaches the FTC fake-reviews rule (16 CFR 465) and misuses Trustpilot and Google marks. `ReviewBadges` is shared, so other pages are probably affected too (not checked).
- **Fix:** render nothing when there are no real reviews, and delete `TOOL_REVIEWS`.

**2. High — the internal-address filter lets hex IPv4-mapped IPv6 through.**
- **Evidence:** in `lib/tools/net-guard.ts:57-69`, the mapped-address check only matches the dotted form (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`). `::ffff:7f00:1` passes, as do `::ffff:a14:64` (10.20.0.100) and `::ffff:a9fe:a9fe` (169.254.169.254).
  - `extractHost` keeps these as-is.
  - Locally, `net.connect(22,'::ffff:7f00:1')` connected, with remote `::ffff:127.0.0.1`.
  - The deployed build has the identical logic.
- **Affected routes:**
  - port-checker (`route.ts:51,60-69`) and mc-status (`:189,216`) allow any port.
  - ssl-checker (port 443 only).
  - http-headers is safe only by accident: `URL.hostname` keeps the brackets, which the host check then rejects.
- **Why it matters:** unauthenticated scanning of the hypervisor's localhost (Proxmox on 8006, Postgres, the app itself) and the customer VM network 10.20.0.0/24.
- **Fix:** normalise with ipaddr.js `.process()` and block `::ffff:0:0/96`, `::/96`, `64:ff9b::/96` and `2002::/16`. Also re-check `socket.remoteAddress` after connecting, or add an nftables egress block for the web process.

**3. High — the latency test only measures Singapore and wrongly says Singapore is the only data centre.**
- **What it measures:**
  - The browser makes one discarded warm-up request to same-origin `/api/tools/ping?warmup=1`.
  - It then makes 15 sequential `GET /api/tools/ping?n=i&_=ts` requests with `cache:no-store`, 120 ms apart.
  - Each sample is `performance.now()` from before `fetch` until after `res.arrayBuffer()` (`LatencyTestTool.tsx:42-47`). The warm-up is excluded.
  - The headline is the plain mean, plus best, worst and jitter (mean difference between consecutive samples). There is no median, and it is not a server-side ping.
  - Every request goes to the one origin: nxeon.cloud has a single A record, 51.79.162.96 (OVH Singapore, the primary node), with no CDN and no AAAA record.
  - Each sample includes about 4–5 ms of nginx plus Next.js handling (measured on the box: time to first byte 4.3–4.7 ms on a reused HTTP/2 connection). It does not include TLS, because the connection is reused.
  - It shows no invented numbers for other regions.
- **The problem:** the tool (`LatencyTestTool.tsx:119-129`) and the page's FAQ structured data (`latency-test/page.tsx:28,58-61`) say "we currently serve from a single Singapore data center". In fact node-2 (fsn1, Germany, 178.63.94.114) is enabled and offered in the deploy wizard, and runs 10 customer servers (5 VPS, 5 game).
- **Why it matters:** a European visitor sees 150–250 ms and is told that is what they would get, when Nxeon can host them in Germany.
- **Related, same problem:** the deploy wizard shows every visitor a fixed "~12 ms" for Singapore and "~70 ms" for Germany with signal bars (`lib/nx/catalog.ts:52-62`, `components/nx/OrderBits.tsx:179-182`). A visitor in the US sees "Singapore ~12 ms".
- **Fix:** add a small no-cache endpoint on each region's node, measure one per region with a median, and use the same probe in the wizard.

**4. High — the server size calculator contradicts Nxeon's real products and prices.**
- **Evidence:** it only reads VPS `Plan` rows (`server-size-calculator/page.tsx:37-43`), yet its buttons go to the game, web-hosting and cloud pages. Default outputs, checked against the database:

| Workload (default scale) | Calculator says | What Nxeon actually sells |
|---|---|---|
| Palworld, 8 players | "Exceeds our largest plan — talk to us" | Palworld 8 GB / 8 players at $21.58 |
| ARK: Survival Ascended, 20 players | Exceeds largest plan | ARK:SA 12 GB / 20 players at $38.86 |
| Minecraft, 10 players | Standard, $18.70 | Minecraft 4 GB / 20 slots at $12.94 |
| Rust, 50 slots | Max, $47.50 | Rust 6 GB / 60 slots at $25.90 |
| CS2, 10 players | Pro (8 GB), $30.22 | CS2 tops out at 4 GB / 24 slots, $24.46 |
| Website | "Starter", $12.78 | /web-hosting's "Starter" is $2.99 |

- **Other problems:** "ARK: Survival Ascended" links to `/ark-server-hosting`, which is the Survival Evolved page (`server-sizing.ts:113-122`). The button uses only `productHref` (`ServerSizeCalculatorTool.tsx:108`), with no link to the chosen plan, even though `deployHref({service:"game", gameFamily, players})` / `{planId}` already exists in `lib/deploy-intent.ts`.
- **Fix:** size games against `GamePlan` for that game, web against `HostingPlan`, and link straight to the deploy wizard.

**5. High — an anonymous visitor who clicks "Register" in the domain generator loses the domain.**
- **Evidence:** the link is `/register?domain=…` (`DomainGeneratorTool.tsx:122-125`), but `app/register/page.tsx:36-43` only reads `next` and `error`, and nothing else reads `domain`. The route comment (`route.ts:58-59`) says the name is "carried through"; it isn't. The same bug is in `components/marketing/DomainChecker.tsx:40`.
- **Fix:** `/register?next=${encodeURIComponent('/dashboard/domains/register?domain='+d)}`.

**6. Medium — the "AI Domain Name Generator" has no AI in production.**
- **Evidence:** `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is not set in the running `nxeon-web` process, `.env`, or the build's `.env`. The live response had `"source":"heuristic"`. The title, meta text and catalog entry all say "AI" (`domain-generator/page.tsx:7,43`, `catalog.ts:24`).
- **What does work:** it degrades cleanly to the built-in word generator (model `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, 20 s timeout) with no errors, but the UI never shows which source produced the names.
- **Fix:** set a funded key, or only say "AI" when `source === "ai"`.

**7. Medium — the domain generator silently ignores every extension after the first two.**
- 12 names × 2 default TLDs = 24, which is exactly `MAX_LOOKUPS` (`domain-suggest.ts:34,37,151-160`; defaults `["com","co"]` in `domain-vocab.ts:193`).
- The live request with com, co and io returned 0 .io results, yet the UI lets you pick up to 6.
- **Fix:** scale the name count to the number of TLDs, or grey out extensions that won't be checked.

**8. Medium — the domain generator can say names are "taken" when they weren't checked.**
- It shows "Every name we tried is already taken" whenever nothing is available (`DomainGeneratorTool.tsx:310-316`), including when every result is "unknown" because the registrar is down or throttled. That contradicts the amber banner just above it.
- A result that is available but has no price is recorded as "taken" (`domain-availability.ts:123-126`).
- **Fix:** base the message on the actual status counts, and map priceless available results to "unknown".

**9. Medium — WHOIS shows the wrong registrar for every .com/.net domain.**
- **Evidence:** the parser's `key.startsWith("registrar")` (`whois/route.ts:67,72`) matches "Registrar WHOIS Server" first. Live github.com showed registrar `whois.markmonitor.com` instead of "MarkMonitor Inc.".
- **Also:** there is no RDAP support (ICANN's standard since January 2025). When IANA gives no referral, IANA's own record is summarised as if it were the domain's.
- **Fix:** match keys exactly; use RDAP with WHOIS as a fallback.

**10. Medium — Minecraft status display problems.**
- MOTDs sent as plain strings keep raw colour codes (`mc-status/route.ts:75`). Live Hypixel shows `§f … §aHypixel Network §c[1.8/26.3]`.
- "Latency" is timed from Singapore and includes the time the server takes to build its status reply (Hypixel: 638 ms), with no "from Singapore" label.
- `Edition: "Java · SRV followed"` is hard-coded (`ToolLanding.tsx:202`), even when no SRV record was followed.

**11. Medium — the /tools hub says "No signup, no limits, no tracking"** (`tools/page.tsx:119`). Every marketing page runs VisitTracker (POST `/api/track`) and the site-wide Meta Pixel, and every API has per-IP limits (for example WHOIS 15/min, domain generator 6/min and 40/hour).

**12. Medium — false feature claims in the related-tools cards** (`tooltemplate/data.ts:18-20`): Port Checker "TCP/UDP" (it only does TCP), DNS "SRV records" (not supported), Latency "Ping our regions" (it pings one).

**13. Low — the latency test fails silently.** `if (!res.ok) continue;` skips both the progress update and the delay. If all 15 requests fail (for example a 429 when many users share one carrier IP; the limit is 240/min per IP), there is no result and no error, and the progress bar freezes. Also: the headline should be a median; the "Nxeon edge" wording is wrong (there is no edge network); the `abort` ref is never set, so there is no cancel.

**14. Low — the "per-target" scan limits never trigger.** In port-checker and mc-status they are keyed by IP plus target at 30/min, which is looser than the per-IP 20/min limit. They do nothing against many IPs scanning one victim; key them on the target alone.

**15. Low — calls to action are generic or overstated.**
- All 15 standard tool pages share one sidebar box linking to `/vps` that promises "a dedicated IPv4" (`ToolShell.tsx:193-203`). Dedicated IP is a $2.99 add-on; 17 of 19 running game servers and 9 of 15 running VPS have none.
- The Minecraft tool's box promises "a dedicated IP" too, and never links to `/free-minecraft`.
- WHOIS, DNS, SSL and HTTP-headers have no link to `/domains` or `/web-hosting`.

**16. Low — rough edges.**
- Every tool calls `res.json()` without a guard, so an nginx HTML error page shows "Unexpected token '<'" (the spinner does stop).
- A null MX record displays as "0\t".
- http-headers rejects URLs with a bracketed IPv6 address.
- The calculator shows the regular USD price, not the intro price or the visitor's display currency.
- The first domain search after a restart took 6.04 s. That equals the 6 s registrar deadline, likely Namecheap's cold pricing cache.
- The domain generator text repeatedly says "our registrar", which clashes with your rule against implying a third-party provider.
